The result highlights the potential of machine learning dynamical phase transitions in nonequilibrium systems.

papers.title: Spatiodynamic inference using vision-based generative modelling
papers.abstract: Biological systems commonly exhibit complex spatiotemporal patterns whose underlying generative mechanisms pose a significant analytical challenge. Traditional approaches to spatiodynamic inference rely on dimensionality reduction through summary statistics, which sacrifice complexity and interdependent structure intrinsic to these data in favor of parameter identifiability. This imposes a fundamental constraint on reliably extracting mechanistic insights from spatiotemporal data, highlighting the need for analytical frameworks that preserve the full richness of these dynamical systems. To address this, we developed a simulation-based inference framework that employs vision transformer-driven variational encoding to generate compact representations of the data, exploiting the inherent contextual dependencies. These representations are subsequently integrated into a likelihood-free Bayesian approach for parameter inference. The central idea is to construct a fine-grained, structured mesh of latent representations from simulated dynamics through systematic exploration of the parameter space. This encoded mesh of latent embeddings then serves as a reference map for retrieving parameter values that correspond to observed data. By integrating generative modeling with Bayesian principles, our approach provides a unified inference framework to identify both spatial and temporal patterns that manifest in multivariate dynamical systems.

papers.title: Constructing Collective Variables Using Invariant Learned Representations
papers.abstract: On the time scales accessible to atomistic numerical modeling, chemical reactions are considered rare events. Therefore, the atomistic simulations are commonly biased along a low-dimensional representation of a chemical reaction in an atomic structure space, i.e., along the collective variables. However, suitable collective variables are often complicated to guess a priori. We propose a novel method of collective variable discovery based on dimensionality reduction of the atomic representation vectors. These linear-scaling and invariant representations can be either fixed (untrained) or learned by supervised training of the end-to-end machine learning potential. The learned representations are expected to reflect not only the structural but also the energetic features of the system that are transferable to all of the reactive transformation covered by the machine learning potential. We demonstrate our approach on four high-barrier reactions ranging from a simple gas-phase hydrogen jump reaction to complex reactions in periodic models of industrially relevant heterogeneous catalysts. High data efficiency, automatized feature extraction, favorable scaling, and retention of inherent invariances are all properties that are expected to enable fast and largely automatic construction of suitable collective variables even in highly complex reactive scenarios such as reactive/catalytic transformations at solid-liquid interfaces.

papers.title: Time-Evolving Dynamical System for Learning Latent Representations of Mouse Visual Neural Activity
papers.research_question: How to extract high-quality latent representations from visual neural activity that capture temporal dynamics and disentangle stimulus-relevant components from internal states?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TE-ViDS, a sequential latent variable model that evolves two parts of latent representations over time to disentangle stimulus-relevant components from internal states in visual neural activity, achieving state-of-the-art decoding performance and providing insights into visual processing.
papers.conclusion: TE-ViDS is markedly competent in extracting stimulus-relevant embeddings from visual neural activity and contributes to the understanding of visual processing mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
TE-ViDS achieves the best decoding performance on natural scenes and natural movies compared to alternative models.
TE-ViDS extracts interpretable latent trajectories that uncover clear underlying neural dynamics.
TE-ViDS provides new insights into differences in visual information processing between subjects and between cortical regions.
The external latent representations are tuned to stimulus-relevant components, while internal latent representations reflect internal states.
The model's performance varies across mouse visual cortical regions, with primary and mid-level regions showing higher decoding performance than high-level regions.
papers.limitation:
In the absence of recorded internal states or behavioral information, it is difficult to quantitatively assess the interpretability of internal latent variables and interpret their functional role.
The model exhibits substantial variability in decoding performance across individual mice, which may be due to variability in neural activity between subjects and trials.
future_direction: Extend the approach to neural data from other species and modalities to investigate broader principles of biological coding mechanisms.
Further exploration is required to consistently construct high-quality stimulus-correlated latent representations across conditions.
papers.abstract: Seeking high-quality representations with latent variable models (LVMs) to reveal the intrinsic correlation between neural activity and behavior or sensory stimuli has attracted much interest. In the study of the biological visual system, naturalistic visual stimuli are inherently high-dimensional and time-dependent, leading to intricate dynamics within visual neural activity. However, most work on LVMs has not explicitly considered neural temporal relationships. To cope with such conditions, we propose Time-Evolving Visual Dynamical System (TE-ViDS), a sequential LVM that decomposes neural activity into low-dimensional latent representations that evolve over time. To better align the model with the characteristics of visual neural activity, we split latent representations into two parts and apply contrastive learning to shape them. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets and real neural datasets from the mouse visual cortex demonstrate that TE-ViDS achieves the best decoding performance on naturalistic scenes/movies, extracts interpretable latent trajectories that uncover clear underlying neural dynamics, and provides new insights into differences in visual information processing between subjects and between cortical regions. In summary, TE-ViDS is markedly competent in extracting stimulus-relevant embeddings from visual neural activity and contributes to the understanding of visual processing mechanisms. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Grasshlw/Time-Evolving-Visual-Dynamical-System.

papers.title: Navigating the Latent Space Dynamics of Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can neural models, specifically autoencoders, be interpreted as dynamical systems, and what properties of the model and data can be revealed by the latent vector field and its attractors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that autoencoders implicitly define a latent vector field whose attractors encode model properties, enabling analysis of generalization and memorization, data-free probing of pretrained models, and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.conclusion: The latent vector field provides a novel and powerful representation for analyzing neural models, revealing internal properties and enabling applications like data-free probing and OOD detection.
papers.key_findings:
Autoencoders define a latent vector field whose attractors correspond to memorized data points or generalized representations, depending on regularization.
During training, the model transitions from memorization to generalization, which is reflected in the evolution of attractors.
Attractors computed from Gaussian noise can recover semantic information from pretrained vision foundation models without any input data.
Trajectories in the latent vector field can distinguish in-distribution from out-of-distribution samples, enabling OOD detection.
The memorization-generalization trade-off is controlled by regularization strength, such as bottleneck dimension.
papers.limitation: The method is primarily demonstrated on autoencoders; extension to other architectures (e.g., SSL models, LLMs) requires further analysis.
future_direction: Study latent vector fields in models beyond autoencoders, such as self-supervised learning models and large language models.
Investigate the impact of architectural elements (e.g., positional embeddings) on the latent dynamics.
Explore the connection between latent dynamics and reasoning in models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks transform high-dimensional data into compact, structured representations, often modeled as elements of a lower dimensional latent space. In this paper, we present an alternative interpretation of neural models as dynamical systems acting on the latent manifold. Specifically, we show that autoencoder models implicitly define a latent vector field on the manifold, derived by iteratively applying the encoding-decoding map, without any additional training. We observe that standard training procedures introduce inductive biases that lead to the emergence of attractor points within this vector field. Drawing on this insight, we propose to leverage the vector field as a representation for the network, providing a novel tool to analyze the properties of the model and the data. This representation enables to: (i) analyze the generalization and memorization regimes of neural models, even throughout training; (ii) extract prior knowledge encoded in the network's parameters from the attractors, without requiring any input data; (iii) identify out-of-distribution samples from their trajectories in the vector field. We further validate our approach on vision foundation models, showcasing the applicability and effectiveness of our method in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Toy Models of Superposition
papers.research_question: Why do neurons sometimes align with interpretable features and sometimes not, and how can neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions (superposition)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that superposition—where neural networks store more sparse features than dimensions—is a real phenomenon, explains polysemanticity, and reveals a phase change and geometric structure in feature representations.
papers.conclusion: Superposition occurs in neural networks, allowing them to represent more features than dimensions, which has important implications for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Superposition is a real, observed phenomenon in neural networks.
Both monosemantic and polysemantic neurons can form.
At least some kinds of computation can be performed in superposition.
Whether features are stored in superposition is governed by a phase change.
Superposition organizes features into geometric structures such as digons, triangles, pentagons, and tetrahedrons.
papers.limitation:
The toy models are simple and it is unclear what to generalize to real networks.
The ReLU hidden layer toy model has a weakness where the model circumvents the activation function if possible.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron - a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. This paper provides a toy model where polysemanticity can be fully understood, arising as a result of models storing additional sparse features in "superposition." We demonstrate the existence of a phase change, a surprising connection to the geometry of uniform polytopes, and evidence of a link to adversarial examples. We also discuss potential implications for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Identifiable Interpretation and Control in Generative Models via Causal Minimality
papers.research_question: Under what theoretical conditions can we reliably identify meaningful, interpretable latent concepts within modern generative models? And what actionable, theoretically-grounded insights can advance both interpretability and controllability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a theoretical framework based on causal minimality that provides conditions under which latent representations in generative models can be identified component-wise, enabling interpretable hierarchical concept graphs and fine-grained control.
papers.conclusion: The experiments illustrate the implications of the theorems and show how a principled, causal understanding can guide the application of established interpretation techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The principle of causal minimality, instantiated as sparsity constraints, enables the extraction of interpretable hierarchical concept graphs from text-to-image diffusion models.
The learned representations under these conditions are component-wise identifiable, meaning they correspond to true latent variables of the data-generating process.
These causally grounded concepts allow for fine-grained model steering, demonstrated in tasks like model unlearning, controllable generation, and multi-level editing.
papers.limitation: The theoretical assumptions, such as causal minimality and smoothness, may not hold universally in practice.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models, while revolutionizing fields like image and text generation, largely operate as opaque black boxes, hindering human understanding, control, and alignment. While methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show remarkable empirical success, they often lack theoretical guarantees, risking subjective insights. Our primary objective is to establish a principled foundation for interpretable generative models. We demonstrate that the principle of causal minimality -- favoring the simplest causal explanation -- can endow the latent representations of diffusion vision and autoregressive language models with clear causal interpretation and robust, component-wise identifiable control. We introduce a novel theoretical framework for hierarchical selection models, where higher-level concepts emerge from the constrained composition of lower-level variables, better capturing the complex dependencies in data generation. Under theoretically derived minimality conditions (manifesting as sparsity or compression constraints), we show that learned representations can be equivalent to the true latent variables of the data-generating process. Empirically, applying these constraints to leading generative models allows us to extract their innate hierarchical concept graphs, offering fresh insights into their internal knowledge organization. Furthermore, these causally grounded concepts serve as levers for fine-grained model steering, paving the way for transparent, reliable systems.

papers.title: Concept Formation and Dynamics of Repeated Inference in Deep Generative Models
papers.research_question: What kinds of inference dynamics does the VAE demonstrate when noise is added to the input data, and how does the dynamics relate to concept formation in the latent space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the repeated inference dynamics in a VAE first approaches the concept (center of a cluster) and then moves to a specific memory, and that with increased noise, the dynamics approaches a more abstract concept. It also shows that sufficient latent variables are needed for this concept attraction and that it correlates with generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: The VAE extracts cluster structures in the data and infers images via the center of each cluster. The dynamics of repeated inference first approaches the concept and then moves to memories, and this behavior is enhanced with sufficient latent variables, which also improves generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The transient dynamics of inference in the VAE's latent space first rapidly approaches the concept (center of a cluster) and then moves away towards a specific memory pattern.
With increased noise in the input, the inference dynamics approaches a more abstract concept (average of all concepts) rather than the specific concept of the cluster.
Orthogonality between concepts in the latent space is necessary for the inference trajectory to be drawn into the concept, and this orthogonality is achieved when the number of latent variables is sufficiently large (around 14 for MNIST).
The generalization performance of the VAE, measured by the variational lower bound on test data, improves when the concept attraction is observed, and the optimal number of latent variables for MNIST is around 14.
The dynamics of repeated inference in the VAE is consistent with associative memory models and neural findings in the visual cortex, suggesting a universal principle.
future_direction: Using other deep generative models to investigate factors influencing the behavior of repeated inferences approaching the concept.
Analyzing the dynamics of repeated inferences with training datasets having more and various hierarchies.
papers.abstract: Deep generative models are reported to be useful in broad applications including image generation. Repeated inference between data space and latent space in these models can denoise cluttered images and improve the quality of inferred results. However, previous studies only qualitatively evaluated image outputs in data space, and the mechanism behind the inference has not been investigated. The purpose of the current study is to numerically analyze changes in activity patterns of neurons in the latent space of a deep generative model called a "variational auto-encoder" (VAE). What kinds of inference dynamics the VAE demonstrates when noise is added to the input data are identified. The VAE embeds a dataset with clear cluster structures in the latent space and the center of each cluster of multiple correlated data points (memories) is referred as the concept. Our study demonstrated that transient dynamics of inference first approaches a concept, and then moves close to a memory. Moreover, the VAE revealed that the inference dynamics approaches a more abstract concept to the extent that the uncertainty of input data increases due to noise. It was demonstrated that by increasing the number of the latent variables, the trend of the inference dynamics to approach a concept can be enhanced, and the generalization ability of the VAE can be improved.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Latent Abstractions in Generative Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How do diffusion-based generative models produce high-dimensional data by implicitly relying on a low-dimensional set of latent abstractions that guide the generative process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a novel theoretical framework based on Nonlinear Filtering that explains how diffusion models implicitly rely on latent abstractions to guide the generative process, and validates it empirically.
papers.conclusion: The Nonlinear Filtering framework offers a theoretical understanding of how diffusion models leverage latent abstractions, and experiments confirm the hierarchical emergence of these abstractions during generation.
papers.key_findings:
Latent abstractions emerge hierarchically in diffusion models, with global attributes (e.g., shape, wall hue) emerging before local details.
Mutual information between the generative process and latent abstractions increases over time, validating the theoretical framework.
The forking protocol demonstrates that once a latent factor emerges, different generative pathways converge to coherent values for that factor.
Linear probing on internal features of the denoising network reveals that latent abstractions are discernible even at high noise levels.
The theory provides a unified perspective on forward and backward diffusion processes as a single Nonlinear Filtering simulation.
papers.limitation: The theoretical framework requires technical assumptions and may encounter singularities at the final time T in the SDE dynamics.
future_direction: Applications in image editing and improved conditional generation.
papers.abstract: In this work we study how diffusion-based generative models produce high-dimensional data, such as an image, by implicitly relying on a manifestation of a low-dimensional set of latent abstractions, that guide the generative process. We present a novel theoretical framework that extends NLF, and that offers a unique perspective on SDE-based generative models. The development of our theory relies on a novel formulation of the joint (state and measurement) dynamics, and an information-theoretic measure of the influence of the system state on the measurement process. According to our theory, diffusion models can be cast as a system of SDE, describing a non-linear filter in which the evolution of unobservable latent abstractions steers the dynamics of an observable measurement process (corresponding to the generative pathways). In addition, we present an empirical study to validate our theory and previous empirical results on the emergence of latent abstractions at different stages of the generative process.

papers.title: Expressive architectures enhance interpretability of dynamics-based neural population models
papers.research_question: Does NODE-based sequential autoencoders more accurately and parsimoniously recover latent dynamical systems from simulated neural activity compared to RNN-based models?
papers.core_contribution: NODE-based sequential autoencoders can recover accurate and parsimonious latent dynamics from simulated neural activity, outperforming RNN-based models in interpretability.
papers.conclusion: NODE-based architectures are superior for interpretable neural population modeling due to their ability to learn accurate dynamics in low-dimensional latent spaces.
papers.key_findings:
NODE-based SAEs achieve similar reconstruction performance with fewer latent dimensions than GRU-based SAEs.
NODE-based SAEs have higher state R^2, indicating better recovery of true latent dynamics without superfluous features.
NODE-based SAEs more effectively recover fixed point properties and eigenvalues of the dynamical systems.
Ablation experiments show that skip connections and MLP capacity in NODEs are key to their superior performance.
RNN-based models struggle to recover accurate dynamics even when they have high reconstruction performance.
papers.limitation:
Global dynamics may be underdetermined from limited sampled trajectories, affecting fixed point recovery.
Models with best reconstruction performance may not concisely capture true dynamics, especially in chaotic systems.
Applicability to real neural data with time-varying dynamics and external inputs is uncertain.
future_direction: Extending the approach to real neural data with inputs and time-varying dynamics.
Testing recovery on partially observed and interacting dynamical systems.
Incorporating techniques from models like LFADS while preserving interpretability.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks that can recover latent dynamics from recorded neural activity may provide a powerful avenue for identifying and interpreting the dynamical motifs underlying biological computation. Given that neural variance alone does not uniquely determine a latent dynamical system, interpretable architectures should prioritize accurate and low-dimensional latent dynamics. In this work, we evaluated the performance of sequential autoencoders (SAEs) in recovering latent chaotic attractors from simulated neural datasets. We found that SAEs with widely-used recurrent neural network (RNN)-based dynamics were unable to infer accurate firing rates at the true latent state dimensionality, and that larger RNNs relied upon dynamical features not present in the data. On the other hand, SAEs with neural ordinary differential equation (NODE)-based dynamics inferred accurate rates at the true latent state dimensionality, while also recovering latent trajectories and fixed point structure. Ablations reveal that this is mainly because NODEs (1) allow use of higher-capacity multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to model the vector field and (2) predict the derivative rather than the next state. Decoupling the capacity of the dynamics model from its latent dimensionality enables NODEs to learn the requisite low-D dynamics where RNN cells fail. Additionally, the fact that the NODE predicts derivatives imposes a useful autoregressive prior on the latent states. The suboptimal interpretability of widely-used RNN-based dynamics may motivate substitution for alternative architectures, such as NODE, that enable learning of accurate dynamics in low-dimensional latent spaces.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of\n Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple types of features (facets) each neuron responds to, and improves activation maximization visualizations with more natural colors and coherent structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization by producing higher quality images and shows the multiple feature facets each neuron detects, providing a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level ones.
Multifaceted feature visualization produces more realistic and interpretable visualizations than previous activation maximization methods.
The method reveals that DNNs learn not only discriminative features but also global structure and context, similar to generative models.
Hidden fully connected layer neurons sometimes represent amalgams of different concepts.
papers.limitation:
The number of facets visualized depends on the manually set parameter k in k-means; automatically determining the true number of facets remains an open problem.
The method does not always reconstruct a proper facet (e.g., for stuffed peppers), possibly because the neuron ignores certain features.
Center-biased regularization is not guaranteed to produce a single object; it only biases optimization toward the center.
future_direction: Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron.
Investigating the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves visualization quality.
Further research into understanding the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons.
papers.abstract:
We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features
each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have
created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which
synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each
neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron
detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted,
in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example,
a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a
storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images
without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating
inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc.
Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of
each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of
images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that
produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images
obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of
image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate
colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus
provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each
neuron.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Inverting Supervised Representations with Autoregressive Neural Density Models
papers.research_question: How can we invert supervised representations to gain insights into the invariances learned by models and to estimate the mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a method for inverting supervised representations using autoregressive neural density models, enabling visualization of model invariances and estimation of mutual information between inputs and intermediate representations.
papers.conclusion: The method facilitates visualization of model invariances and provides a scalable quantitative estimate of the amount of information preserved by a network.
papers.key_findings:
Mutual information between inputs and network layers decreases through successive layers, with the biggest reduction between CONV1 and CONV2.
Global pooling induces translation invariance in convolutional networks, while preserving style and rotation information.
Mutual information initially increases and then decreases over the course of training, supporting the information bottleneck theory.
Inversion models provide better calibration of variability compared to SGAN and nearest neighbor methods.
The method allows analysis of architectural choices by revealing invariances learned by different network architectures.
papers.limitation: Density estimation is challenging in higher dimensions, and it is not known how well a given model represents the true density.
future_direction: Improving the method as neural density models improve to achieve tighter mutual information bounds and more representative samples.
papers.abstract: We present a method for feature interpretation that makes use of recent advances in autoregressive density estimation models to invert model representations. We train generative inversion models to express a distribution over input features conditioned on intermediate model representations. Insights into the invariances learned by supervised models can be gained by viewing samples from these inversion models. In addition, we can use these inversion models to estimate the mutual information between a model’s inputs and its intermediate representations, thus quantifying the amount of information preserved by the network at different stages. Using this method we examine the types of information preserved at different layers of convolutional neural networks, and explore the invariances induced by different architectural choices. Finally we show that the mutual information between inputs and network layers initially increases and then decreases over the course of training, supporting recent work by Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby (2017) on the information bottleneck theory of deep learning.

papers.title: Extending Activation Steering to Broad Skills and Multiple Behaviours
papers.research_question: Can we extend activation steering to broad skills and multiple behaviours?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can be applied to broad skills (coding) with similar effectiveness as narrow skills, and simultaneous injection of multiple steering vectors at different layers is more promising than combining them into a single vector.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can be extended to broad skills and multiple behaviours, with simultaneous steering being a promising direction.
papers.key_findings:
Steering to reduce general coding ability is competitive with steering to reduce Python-specific ability.
Individual steering vectors for behaviours like myopia and wealth-seeking are effective.
Combining multiple steering vectors into one vector is largely unsuccessful.
Simultaneous injection of individual steering vectors at different layers is promising and has minor alignment tax.
Steering at layer 0 for coding ability had an opposite effect, possibly due to copy suppression.
papers.limitation:
The flexibility of activation steering makes finding optimal setups non-trivial.
It is unclear whether reductions in matching scores (e.g., a 20% reduction in coding accuracy) translate to real-world risk reduction.
future_direction: Testing with other models to understand the general working of activation steering.
Using different injection coefficients for different steering vectors in simultaneous steering.
Generating and injecting steering vectors at different places within a layer (e.g., attention and MLP components).
Steering against alternative programming languages to further investigate broad steering.
papers.abstract: Current large language models have dangerous capabilities, which are likely to become more problematic in the future. Activation steering techniques can be used to reduce risks from these capabilities. In this paper, we investigate the efficacy of activation steering for broad skills and multiple behaviours. First, by comparing the effects of reducing performance on general coding ability and Python-specific ability, we find that steering broader skills is competitive to steering narrower skills. Second, we steer models to become more or less myopic and wealth-seeking, among other behaviours. In our experiments, combining steering vectors for multiple different behaviours into one steering vector is largely unsuccessful. On the other hand, injecting individual steering vectors at different places in a model simultaneously is promising.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Restyling Unsupervised Concept Based Interpretable Networks with Generative Models
papers.research_question: How can we improve the visualization and interpretation of learnt unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks for large-scale images?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes VisCoIN, a novel architecture for unsupervised concept-based interpretable networks that maps concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model, enabling high-quality visualization and interactive interpretation of learnt concepts.
papers.conclusion: VisCoIN effectively leverages pretrained generative models to improve visualization and interpretation of unsupervised concepts in concept-based interpretable networks, achieving high prediction performance and learning more faithful and consistent concepts.
papers.key_findings:
VisCoIN achieves comparable prediction accuracy to baseline methods while improving reconstruction fidelity and perceptual similarity.
The learnt concepts in VisCoIN are more faithful and consistent compared to previous unsupervised CoINs.
The visualization pipeline based on the generative model allows for granular and interactive interpretation of concepts by modifying concept activations and observing changes in generated images.
papers.limitation:
Cannot guarantee that concepts precisely correspond to human concepts and may encode additional information.
System quality is limited by the quality of the pretrained generative model.
Linear trajectories in latent space may not be optimal for latent traversals.
papers.abstract: Developing inherently interpretable models for prediction has gained prominence in recent years. A subclass of these models, wherein the interpretable network relies on learning high-level concepts, are valued because of closeness of concept representations to human communication. However, the visualization and understanding of the learnt unsupervised dictionary of concepts encounters major limitations, especially for large-scale images. We propose here a novel method that relies on mapping the concept features to the latent space of a pretrained generative model. The use of a generative model enables high quality visualization, and lays out an intuitive and interactive procedure for better interpretation of the learnt concepts by imputing concept activations and visualizing generated modifications. Furthermore, leveraging pretrained generative models has the additional advantage of making the training of the system more efficient. We quantitatively ascertain the efficacy of our method in terms of accuracy of the interpretable prediction network, fidelity of reconstruction, as well as faithfulness and consistency of learnt concepts. The experiments are conducted on multiple image recognition benchmarks for large-scale images. Project page available at https://jayneelparekh.github.io/VisCoIN_project_page/

papers.title: Predictive learning as a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations
papers.research_question: Does learning to predict future observations cause neural networks to extract low-dimensional latent structure from their sensory inputs?
papers.core_contribution: Predictive learning in neural networks leads to the emergence of low-dimensional internal representations that linearly encode the latent variables of the environment, a process that can be quantified using novel metrics like latent signal transfer and dimensionality gain.
papers.conclusion: Predictive learning is a network mechanism for extracting low-dimensional latent space representations from high-dimensional sensory inputs, which can be characterized by the introduced metrics and analytical tools.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive learning causes neural networks to form low-dimensional representations that map the latent structure of the sensory environment.
Latent space signal transfer occurs during learning, where latent variables become increasingly linearly decodable from the top principal components of the neural representation.
Dimensionality gain (the ratio of linear to nonlinear dimensionality) increases during predictive learning, indicating the extraction of a low-dimensional manifold from high-dimensional observations.
Predictive learning leads to the emergence of neurons with localized activations on the manifold (manifold cells).
Representations formed by predictive learning are more structured and better reflect the latent space than those formed by autoencoding (non-predictive learning).
future_direction: Further testing of the predictive learning framework in neural data.
Application of the framework to additional tasks beyond spatial exploration and arm-reaching.
Investigation of predictive learning as a general principle for representation formation in both biological and artificial neural networks.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks have recently achieved many successes in solving sequential processing and planning tasks. Their success is often ascribed to the emergence of the task's low-dimensional latent structure in the network activity - i.e., in the learned neural representations. Here, we investigate the hypothesis that a means for generating representations with easily accessed low-dimensional latent structure, possibly reflecting an underlying semantic organization, is through learning to predict observations about the world. Specifically, we ask whether and when network mechanisms for sensory prediction coincide with those for extracting the underlying latent variables. Using a recurrent neural network model trained to predict a sequence of observations we show that network dynamics exhibit low-dimensional but nonlinearly transformed representations of sensory inputs that map the latent structure of the sensory environment. We quantify these results using nonlinear measures of intrinsic dimensionality and linear decodability of latent variables, and provide mathematical arguments for why such useful predictive representations emerge. We focus throughout on how our results can aid the analysis and interpretation of experimental data.

papers.title: Interpretable statistical representations of neural population dynamics and geometry
papers.research_question: How can we learn interpretable and consistent latent representations of neural population dynamics that evolve on low-dimensional manifolds, and how can we compare these dynamics across conditions, networks, and animals?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARBLE, an unsupervised geometric deep learning method that learns interpretable latent representations of neural population dynamics by decomposing them into local flow fields, enabling consistent comparison of dynamics across networks and animals.
papers.conclusion: Our results suggest that manifold structure provides a powerful inductive bias to develop powerful decoding algorithms and assimilate data across experiments.
papers.key_findings:
MARBLE discovers low-dimensional latent representations that parametrize high-dimensional neural dynamics during gain modulation, decision-making, and changes in internal state.
MARBLE representations are consistent across neural networks and animals, enabling robust comparison of cognitive computations.
MARBLE outperforms current representation learning approaches (CEBRA, LFADS) in within- and across-animal decoding accuracy.
MARBLE can detect dynamical events such as bifurcations in RNNs corresponding to loss of task performance.
MARBLE can reveal the global geometric structure of latent states (e.g., circular arrangement for reaching directions) without behavioral supervision.
papers.abstract: The dynamics of neuron populations commonly evolve on low-dimensional manifolds. Thus, we need methods that learn the dynamical processes over neural manifolds to infer interpretable and consistent latent representations. We introduce a representation learning method, MARBLE, that decomposes on-manifold dynamics into local flow fields and maps them into a common latent space using unsupervised geometric deep learning. In simulated non-linear dynamical systems, recurrent neural networks, and experimental single-neuron recordings from primates and rodents, we discover emergent low-dimensional latent representations that parametrise high-dimensional neural dynamics during gain modulation, decision-making, and changes in the internal state. These representations are consistent across neural networks and animals, enabling the robust comparison of cognitive computations. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates state-of-the-art within- and across-animal decoding accuracy of MARBLE compared with current representation learning approaches, with minimal user input. Our results suggest that manifold structure provides a powerful inductive bias to develop powerful decoding algorithms and assimilate data across experiments.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Deep Neural Networks and Visuo-Semantic Models Explain Complementary Components of Human Ventral-Stream Representational Dynamics
papers.research_question: What representational features in human ventral-stream neural dynamics are not accounted for by deep neural networks, and can visuo-semantic models explain additional variance?
papers.core_contribution: DNNs and visuo-semantic models explain complementary components of human ventral-stream representational dynamics, with DNNs better explaining lower-level visual areas early and visuo-semantic models better explaining higher-level areas later.
papers.conclusion: Current DNNs fail to fully capture dynamic representations in higher-level human visual cortex, and visuo-semantic models account for additional structured variance, suggesting a path for model improvement.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs explain more variance in lower-level visual areas (V1-V3) starting at 66 ms after stimulus onset.
Visuo-semantic models explain more variance in higher-level visual areas (IT/PHC) starting at 146 ms after stimulus onset.
Object parts and basic categories are the visuo-semantic features that drive the advantage over DNNs.
The relative importance of DNN versus visuo-semantic features reverses along the ventral stream over space and time.
papers.limitation: Visuo-semantic models are not image-computable and are based on human-generated labels, so how the brain computes these labels remains unknown.
future_direction: Study visual perception under challenging viewing conditions, including occlusion and clutter.
Provide DNNs with a more human-like visual diet and learning objectives to improve their match to human neural representations.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are promising models of the cortical computations supporting human object recognition. However, despite their ability to explain a significant portion of variance in neural data, the agreement between models and brain representational dynamics is far from perfect. We address this issue by asking which representational features are currently unaccounted for in neural time series data, estimated for multiple areas of the ventral stream via source-reconstructed magnetoencephalography data acquired in human participants (nine females, six males) during object viewing. We focus on the ability of visuo-semantic models, consisting of human-generated labels of object features and categories, to explain variance beyond the explanatory power of DNNs alone. We report a gradual reversal in the relative importance of DNN versus visuo-semantic features as ventral-stream object representations unfold over space and time. Although lower-level visual areas are better explained by DNN features starting early in time (at 66 ms after stimulus onset), higher-level cortical dynamics are best accounted for by visuo-semantic features starting later in time (at 146 ms after stimulus onset). Among the visuo-semantic features, object parts and basic categories drive the advantage over DNNs. These results show that a significant component of the variance unexplained by DNNs in higher-level cortical dynamics is structured and can be explained by readily nameable aspects of the objects. We conclude that current DNNs fail to fully capture dynamic representations in higher-level human visual cortex and suggest a path toward more accurate models of ventral-stream computations.SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT When we view objects such as faces and cars in our visual environment, their neural representations dynamically unfold over time at a millisecond scale. These dynamics reflect the cortical computations that support fast and robust object recognition. DNNs have emerged as a promising framework for modeling these computations but cannot yet fully account for the neural dynamics. Using magnetoencephalography data acquired in human observers during object viewing, we show that readily nameable aspects of objects, such as 'eye', 'wheel', and 'face', can account for variance in the neural dynamics over and above DNNs. These findings suggest that DNNs and humans may in part rely on different object features for visual recognition and provide guidelines for model improvement.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Understanding Representation Dynamics of Diffusion Models via Low-Dimensional Modeling
papers.research_question: What causes the unimodal representation dynamics in diffusion models, and how does it relate to model generalization?
