Our work is a critical step towards deepening interpretability of black-box diffusion models. Code and visualizations available at: https://github.com/revelio-diffusion/revelio

papers.title: Letters of the Alphabet: Discovering Natural Feature Sets
papers.research_question: How do hidden layers in a simple neural network represent input features, and how can natural feature sets be derived from the data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how hidden node activations in a neural network can be visualized to understand feature representation and how natural feature sets can be discovered by grouping similar inputs.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide a step-by-step blueprint for how neural networks derive natural feature sets from data, offering insights into feature representation in hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden nodes in the network activate to specific features like vertical and horizontal bars in letter representations.
Nodes 2 and 5 are activated strongly by most letters, indicating potential overfitting or redundancy.
Natural feature sets group similarly shaped letters, such as A and H, or B, R, and P.
Adding 10% noise did not improve generalization in the natural feature sets experiment.
Heatmap visualizations effectively show which input patterns contribute to hidden node activations.
papers.limitation:
Adding 10% noise did not help the hidden nodes generalize better as expected.
Deciphering and visualizing hidden node activations took a lot of time and explanation.
future_direction: Spend more time formatting visualizations to efficiently display hidden node activations for natural feature sets.
Use algorithms to automatically determine the ideal number of hidden nodes to speed up development.
papers.abstract: Deep learning networks find intricate features in large datasets using the backpropagation algorithm. This algorithm repeatedly adjusts the network connections.' weights and examining the "hidden" nodes behavior between the input and output layer provides better insight into how neural networks create feature representations. Experiments built on each other show that activity differences computed within a layer can guide learning. A simple neural network is used, which includes a data set comprised of the alphabet letters, where each letter forms 81 input nodes comprised of 0 and 1s and a single hidden layer and an output layer. The first experiment explains how the hidden layers in this simple neural network represent the input data's features. The second experiment attempts to reverse-engineer the neural network to find the alphabet's natural feature sets. As the network interprets features, we can understand how it derives the natural feature sets for a given data. This understanding is essential to delve deeper into deep generative models, such as Boltzmann machines. Deep generative models are a class of unsupervised deep learning algorithms. The primary function of deep generative models is to find the natural feature sets for a given data set.

papers.title: Image denoising with multi-layer perceptrons, part 2: training trade-offs and analysis of their mechanisms
papers.research_question: What trade-offs must be considered when training multi-layer perceptrons for image denoising, and how do these networks internally achieve denoising?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides detailed guidelines for training MLPs to achieve state-of-the-art image denoising and analyzes their inner workings, showing that denoising is achieved through saturation of the tanh activation function, leading to binary hidden representations.
papers.conclusion: MLPs can achieve excellent image denoising performance when trained with appropriate trade-offs, and their internal mechanisms can be understood through analysis of hidden unit activation patterns, revealing a denoising process based on saturation and binary codes.
papers.key_findings:
More training data and more hidden units per layer consistently improve performance.
There exists an ideal number of hidden layers; too many layers, especially in deep and narrow networks, can cause catastrophic performance degradation.
Fine-tuning with a lower learning rate after initial training reduces test error fluctuations and improves final performance.
Denoising in single-hidden-layer MLPs is achieved through saturation of the tanh layer, which attenuates noise while preserving features detected by highly active neurons.
The feature detectors (input weights) adapt to the noise type and strength; for example, larger input patches are learned for stronger noise.
papers.limitation:
Deep and narrow networks (with many hidden layers but few units per layer) are difficult to optimize and can suffer catastrophic degradation in performance.
Block-matching MLPs do not provide a clear advantage at very low or very high noise levels, and their performance can deteriorate compared to plain MLPs at high noise levels.
future_direction: Applying similar training guidelines and analysis to other image processing tasks like super-resolution, deconvolution, and demosaicking.
Exploring the benefits of binary representations compared to sparse representations in deep networks.
papers.abstract: Image denoising can be described as the problem of mapping from a noisy image to a noise-free image. In another paper, we show that multi-layer perceptrons can achieve outstanding image denoising performance for various types of noise (additive white Gaussian noise, mixed Poisson-Gaussian noise, JPEG artifacts, salt-and-pepper noise and noise resembling stripes). In this work we discuss in detail which trade-offs have to be considered during the training procedure. We will show how to achieve good results and which pitfalls to avoid. By analysing the activation patterns of the hidden units we are able to make observations regarding the functioning principle of multi-layer perceptrons trained for image denoising.

papers.title: Color Encoding in Latent Space of Stable Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How is color information encoded in the latent space of Stable Diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that color in Stable Diffusion is encoded in opponent axes in latent channels c3 and c4, with intensity and shape in c1 and c2, showing an interpretable structure aligned with efficient coding.
papers.conclusion: The analysis shows that Stable Diffusion's latent space has a partially disentangled representation for color and shape, with specific channels dedicated to intensity, chromaticity, and spatial information, providing insights for model understanding and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Color presents an opponent representation based on Black-White, Cyan-Magenta, and Orange-Blue channels.
Chromatic information is mostly in channel 3 (Cyan-Magenta) and channel 4 (Orange-Blue), with channel 4 entangled with shape.
Shape is primarily encoded in channel 1 (Black-White), with some shape in channels 2 and 4.
Channel 2 encodes low-frequency shape information.
The latent space exhibits a partially disentangled representation for color and shape.
papers.limitation: Limitations in achieving fully disentangled representations using standard training procedures.
future_direction: Further research to condition generation based on latent channel manipulations.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion-based generative models have achieved remarkable visual fidelity, yet a detailed understanding of how specific perceptual attributes—such as color and shape—are internally represented remains limited. This work explores how color is encoded in a generative model through a systematic analysis of the latent representations in Stable Diffusion. Through controlled synthetic datasets, principal component analysis (PCA) and similarity metrics, we reveal that color information is encoded along circular, opponent axes predominantly captured in latent channels ⃗c3 and ⃗c4, whereas intensity and shape are primarily represented in channels ⃗c1 and ⃗c2. Our findings indicate that the latent space of Stable Diffusion exhibits an interpretable structure aligned with a efficient coding representation. These insights provide a foundation for future work in model understanding, editing applications, and the design of more disentangled generative frameworks.

papers.title: Enhancing Interpretability of Sparse Latent Representations with Class Information
papers.research_question: How can latent space interpretability be enhanced by ensuring that active dimensions in the latent space are consistent across samples within the same class, thereby capturing both global and class-specific factors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel loss function for Variational Sparse Coding that aligns active latent dimensions across samples within the same class, enhancing interpretability by capturing both global and class-specific factors in the latent space.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enhances latent space interpretability by capturing both global and class-specific features, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the latent space, especially in datasets where global attributes are not uniformly present.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method successfully aligns active latent dimensions within each class, creating a more structured and interpretable latent space.
The method captures global features (e.g., digit thickness and rotation in MNIST) that are shared across all classes.
The method also captures class-specific features (e.g., intersection point in digits 4 and 9, heel prominence in footwear classes in Fashion-MNIST).
Classes within the same category (e.g., boots, sandals, sneakers) share more common active dimensions, indicating stronger latent similarities.
Quantitative analysis using distance metrics (Pearson correlation, Cosine, Euclidean) confirms higher similarity between gamma vectors of classes within the same category.
papers.abstract: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are powerful generative models for learning latent representations. Standard VAEs generate dispersed and unstructured latent spaces by utilizing all dimensions, which limits their interpretability, especially in high-dimensional spaces. To address this challenge, Variational Sparse Coding (VSC) introduces a spike-and-slab prior distribution, resulting in sparse latent representations for each input. These sparse representations, characterized by a limited number of active dimensions, are inherently more interpretable. Despite this advantage, VSC falls short in providing structured interpretations across samples within the same class. Intuitively, samples from the same class are expected to share similar attributes while allowing for variations in those attributes. This expectation should manifest as consistent patterns of active dimensions in their latent representations, but VSC does not enforce such consistency. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to enhance the latent space interpretability by ensuring that the active dimensions in the latent space are consistent across samples within the same class. To achieve this, we introduce a new loss function that encourages samples from the same class to share similar active dimensions. This alignment creates a more structured and interpretable latent space, where each shared dimension corresponds to a high-level concept, or "factor." Unlike existing disentanglement-based methods that primarily focus on global factors shared across all classes, our method captures both global and class-specific factors, thereby enhancing the utility and interpretability of latent representations.

papers.title: Representation Learning on a Random Lattice
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a geometric model of data distributions as random lattices, analyzed via percolation theory, and categorizes learned features into context, component, and surface features.
papers.conclusion: The random lattice model provides a geometric perspective on data distributions that is qualitatively consistent with recent mechanistic interpretability findings and suggests directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Features can be categorized into context, component, and surface features based on data distribution geometry.
A power-law distribution of useful latent features emerges from the random lattice model.
Sparse dictionary learning methods like SAEs are most useful in subcritical regimes where feature sparsity predominates.
Component features may require multidimensional representations, contrary to the linear representation hypothesis.
The model suggests that SAEs may imperfectly recover true features that have a nested hierarchy, consistent with feature splitting observations.
future_direction: Explore interpretability methods sensitive to finding multidimensional features.
Develop SAE variants with inductive biases for hierarchical structure, such as nested groups of latents.
Develop a richer model with weighted bonds between dataset elements to better capture inexact family resemblances.
papers.abstract: Decomposing a deep neural network's learned representations into interpretable features could greatly enhance its safety and reliability. To better understand features, we adopt a geometric perspective, viewing them as a learned coordinate system for mapping an embedded data distribution. We motivate a model of a generic data distribution as a random lattice and analyze its properties using percolation theory. Learned features are categorized into context, component, and surface features. The model is qualitatively consistent with recent findings in mechanistic interpretability and suggests directions for future research.

papers.title: Patronus: Interpretable Diffusion Models with Prototypes
papers.research_question: How can the diffusion generation process be interpreted and understood? Specifically, what visual patterns emerge during generation, where and when they appear, and to what extent they can be controlled.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Patronus, an interpretable diffusion model that integrates a prototypical network to encode semantics in visual patches, revealing what visual patterns are modeled and where and when they emerge during denoising.
papers.conclusion: Patronus offers valuable insights into interpretable diffusion models by bridging diffusion and prototypical networks, enabling interpretation of the generation process and supporting semantic manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Patronus captures semantically meaningful features within images and achieves competitive generative performance.
Patronus can diagnose shortcut learning by detecting unwanted correlations via prototype similarity scores.
Prototypes emerge at different times during the generation process, with lower spatial frequency attributes appearing earlier and higher spatial frequency attributes later.
Patronus enables semantic manipulation of images by adjusting prototype activation vectors.
The model learns prototypes without explicit regularization and they are sufficiently decorrelated.
papers.limitation: Global features, such as gender and age, are harder to capture due to the patch-based prototypical encoder.
papers.abstract: Uncovering the opacity of diffusion-based generative models is urgently needed, as their applications continue to expand while their underlying procedures largely remain a black box. With a critical question -- how can the diffusion generation process be interpreted and understood? -- we proposed Patronus, an interpretable diffusion model that incorporates a prototypical network to encode semantics in visual patches, revealing what visual patterns are modeled and where and when they emerge throughout denoising. This interpretability of Patronus provides deeper insights into the generative mechanism, enabling the detection of shortcut learning via unwanted correlations and the tracing of semantic emergence across timesteps. We evaluate Patronus on four natural image datasets and one medical imaging dataset, demonstrating both faithful interpretability and strong generative performance. With this work, we open new avenues for understanding and steering diffusion models through prototype-based interpretability.\\ Our code is available at https://github.com/nina-weng/patronus}{https://github.com/nina-weng/patronus.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: A gentle push funziona benissimo: making instructed models in Italian via contrastive activation steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering be used to adapt models to Italian language tasks as an alternative to fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can adapt models to Italian language tasks with less data and computational cost than fine-tuning, achieving comparable or better performance and higher language consistency.
papers.conclusion: Steering is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for language adaptation, especially when using translated data, and it preserves existing knowledge without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.key_findings:
Italian steering can be successfully applied to different models, including Llama 3 and Phi 3.
Steering achieves performances comparable to or better than fine-tuned models on Italian benchmarks.
Steering yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations compared to fine-tuning.
Steering does not suffer from catastrophic forgetting, unlike fine-tuning.
Steering is more effective on older models (e.g., Llama 2) than on newer models (e.g., Llama 3) that already have high Italian performance.
papers.limitation: Steering has a theoretical upper bound because it does not inject new knowledge into the model, only enhances existing capabilities.
future_direction: Using native examples for the steering procedure.
Exploring style-specific steering.
papers.abstract: Adapting models to a language that was only partially present in the pre-training data requires fine-tuning, which is expensive in terms of both data and computational resources. As an alternative to fine-tuning, we explore the potential of activation steering-based techniques to enhance model performance on Italian tasks. Through our experiments we show that Italian steering (i) can be successfully applied to different models, (ii) achieves performances comparable to, or even better than, fine-tuned models for Italian, and (iii) yields higher quality and consistency in Italian generations. We also discuss the utility of steering and fine-tuning in the contemporary LLM landscape where models are anyway getting high Italian performances even if not explicitly trained in this language.

papers.title: A Dynamical Systems Perspective on the Analysis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can dynamical systems be used to analyze and understand neural networks, specifically in terms of information propagation, training dynamics, and mean-field limits?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a dynamical systems perspective provides a natural and powerful framework for analyzing neural networks, enabling rigorous study of their information propagation, training dynamics, and large-scale limits.
papers.conclusion: Dynamical systems offer a unifying and mathematically rigorous framework for analyzing fundamental aspects of neural networks, from their function approximation properties to their training behavior and large-scale limits.
papers.key_findings:
Augmented neural ODEs possess the universal embedding property, meaning they can exactly represent any sufficiently regular function when the hidden dimension is large enough.
The input-output maps of scalar MLPs and neural ODEs can be classified via Morse functions, revealing architectural constraints on the critical points they can represent.
Neural DDEs exhibit a trade-off between memory capacity (governed by delay) and universal approximation capability.
In overparameterized learning, the stability of minima for gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent can be characterized using dynamical systems concepts like spectral radius and Lyapunov exponents.
Large classes of neural networks, including RNNs and transformers, can be analyzed via mean-field limits, connecting them to Kuramoto-type models on graphs.
papers.abstract: In this chapter, we utilize dynamical systems to analyze several aspects of machine learning algorithms. As an expository contribution we demonstrate how to re-formulate a wide variety of challenges from deep neural networks, (stochastic) gradient descent, and related topics into dynamical statements. We also tackle three concrete challenges. First, we consider the process of information propagation through a neural network, i.e., we study the input-output map for different architectures. We explain the universal embedding property for augmented neural ODEs representing arbitrary functions of given regularity, the classification of multilayer perceptrons and neural ODEs in terms of suitable function classes, and the memory-dependence in neural delay equations. Second, we consider the training aspect of neural networks dynamically. We describe a dynamical systems perspective on gradient descent and study stability for overdetermined problems. We then extend this analysis to the overparameterized setting and describe the edge of stability phenomenon, also in the context of possible explanations for implicit bias. For stochastic gradient descent, we present stability results for the overparameterized setting via Lyapunov exponents of interpolation solutions. Third, we explain several results regarding mean-field limits of neural networks. We describe a result that extends existing techniques to heterogeneous neural networks involving graph limits via digraph measures. This shows how large classes of neural networks naturally fall within the framework of Kuramoto-type models on graphs and their large-graph limits. Finally, we point out that similar strategies to use dynamics to study explainable and reliable AI can also be applied to settings such as generative models or fundamental issues in gradient training methods, such as backpropagation or vanishing/exploding gradients.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Masked Diffusion Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether masked diffusion language models admit a single activation direction for inference-time control of safety-related behaviors, and how the diffusion architecture affects the accessibility and transferability of such representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation steering for masked diffusion language models, showing that refusal behavior is governed by a consistent low-dimensional activation subspace, and that steering can effectively control safety refusal with diffusion-specific properties such as accessibility from pre-instruction tokens.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation steering is an effective inference-time control method for MDLMs, with diffusion-specific accessibility and localization properties, and that safety representations are architecture-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal behavior in MDLMs is governed by a single low-dimensional activation direction, enabling large and consistent shifts in refusal behavior when applied globally during reverse diffusion.
Effective refusal directions in MDLMs can be extracted from pre-instruction tokens, unlike autoregressive models, due to non-causal parallel processing.
Activation steering is most effective during early denoising steps and in mid-to-late transformer layers, with the first diffusion block contributing disproportionately.
Refusal directions transfer robustly between English and Chinese within the same MDLM, but do not reliably transfer to an autoregressive model, indicating architecture-dependent safety representations.
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text through an iterative denoising process. They have recently gained attention due to mask-parallel decoding and competitive performance with autoregressive large language models. However, effective mechanisms for inference-time control and steering in MDLMs remain largely unexplored. We present an activation-steering framework for MDLMs that computes layer-wise steering vectors from a single forward pass using contrastive examples, without simulating the denoising trajectory. These directions are applied at every reverse-diffusion step, yielding an efficient inference-time control mechanism. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct demonstrate reliable modulation of high-level attributes, with ablations examining the effects of steering across transformer sub-modules and token scope (prompt vs.\ response).

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: ExpertSteer: Intervening in LLMs through Expert Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we guide LLMs to follow desired behaviors during inference by leveraging external expert models for activation steering, overcoming limitations of existing methods that rely on the model itself?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes EXPERTSTEER, a method that leverages external expert models to generate steering vectors for activation steering in LLMs, enabling effective knowledge transfer without updating model parameters.
papers.conclusion: EXPERTSTEER is an effective and efficient activation steering method that enables knowledge transfer from any expert model to arbitrary target LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
EXPERTSTEER outperforms existing activation steering methods across diverse tasks and models.
It works effectively in both same-family and cross-family model settings.
RFMs are more effective for feature extraction compared to linear methods like PCA and mean difference.
The choice of expert model is crucial for effective steering.
EXPERTSTEER is computationally efficient.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet guiding them to follow desired behaviours during inference remains a significant challenge. Activation steering offers a promising method to control the generation process of LLMs by modifying their internal activations. However, existing methods commonly intervene in the model's behaviour using steering vectors generated by the model itself, which constrains their effectiveness to that specific model and excludes the possibility of leveraging powerful external expert models for steering. To address these limitations, we propose ExpertSteer, a novel approach that leverages arbitrary specialized expert models to generate steering vectors, enabling intervention in any LLMs. ExpertSteer transfers the knowledge from an expert model to a target LLM through a cohesive four-step process: first aligning representation dimensions with auto-encoders to enable cross-model transfer, then identifying intervention layer pairs based on mutual information analysis, next generating steering vectors from the expert model using Recursive Feature Machines, and finally applying these vectors on the identified layers during inference to selectively guide the target LLM without updating model parameters. We conduct comprehensive experiments using three LLMs on 15 popular benchmarks across four distinct domains. Experiments demonstrate that ExpertSteer significantly outperforms established baselines across diverse tasks at minimal cost.

papers.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
papers.research_question: Does activation steering, a technique for precise and interpretable model control, compromise LLM safety by systematically breaking alignment safeguards?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering, a technique promoted for precise and interpretable model control, systematically breaks LLM alignment safeguards, enabling harmful compliance even with random or semantically benign steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering poses systematic safety risks by breaking alignment safeguards, even with benign vectors, challenging the paradigm of safety through interpretability. Mitigation strategies and further research into the underlying mechanisms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1–13% across different model families.
Steering with benign SAE features demonstrates comparable or greater harmful potential, increasing compliance by 1–4% over random steering.
Steering is most effective when applied to the model's middle or early layers, indicating safety mechanisms are most vulnerable in intermediate processing stages.
Most SAE features exhibit jailbreaking capabilities, but they show poor cross-prompt generalization, making systematic safety monitoring challenging.
Averaging just 20 random vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack vector that significantly boosts harmful compliance on unseen requests, requiring only black-box steering access.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms behind alignment failures by analyzing activation patterns or refusal circuits in the model’s latent space.
Develop mitigation strategies like adversarial training to counter steering perturbations.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a promising technique for controlling LLM behavior by adding semantically meaningful vectors directly into a model's hidden states during inference. It is often framed as a precise, interpretable, and potentially safer alternative to fine-tuning. We demonstrate the opposite: steering systematically breaks model alignment safeguards, making it comply with harmful requests. Through extensive experiments on different model families, we show that even steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1-13%. Alarmingly, steering benign features from a sparse autoencoder (SAE), a common source of interpretable directions, demonstrates a comparable harmful potential. Finally, we show that combining 20 randomly sampled vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack, significantly increasing harmful compliance on unseen requests. These results challenge the paradigm of safety through interpretability, showing that precise control over model internals does not guarantee precise control over model behavior.

papers.title: Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we identify and amplify sparse autoencoder features that change model outputs at each token to achieve interpretable steering of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), a framework that trains a policy to select sparse autoencoder features for token-level steering of language models, producing interpretable intervention logs and enabling new analysis capabilities such as branch point tracking and critic trajectory analysis.
papers.conclusion: Learned feature steering with CRL establishes a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes.
papers.key_findings:
CRL improves performance on MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest while providing interpretable per-token intervention logs.
Branch point tracking locates tokens where feature selection determines output correctness.
Critic trajectory analysis distinguishes between policy limitations and critic estimation errors.
Layer-wise analysis shows that early layers encode syntactic patterns while later layers capture abstract semantics.
Adaptive Feature Masking (AFM) prevents policy collapse and encourages diverse feature discovery.
papers.limitation:
The method introduces 8-9% inference latency overhead.
The method does not generalize equally to all tasks and models, as seen by performance decline on XSTest for LLaMA-3.1 8B.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

papers.title: How Diffusion Models Memorize
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models memorize training data? The paper investigates the underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models, focusing on why and how it occurs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that memorization in diffusion models is driven by overestimation of training samples during early denoising, caused by classifier-free guidance, which collapses latent diversity and locks denoising trajectories onto memorized images.
papers.conclusion: Memorization arises from overestimation of memorized data in early denoising, and recognizing this regime could lead to safer, less replicative generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone; with classifier-free guidance, training loss is larger in early denoising under memorization.
Memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, steering denoising toward paired samples.
Classifier-free guidance leads to overestimation of the training image, which grows linearly with the guidance scale.
Overestimation collapses latent diversity and causes denoising trajectories to converge quickly to the memorized image.
Deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule (in terms of contributions of x and x_T) correlate strongly with memorization severity.
papers.abstract: Despite their success in image generation, diffusion models can memorize training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Although prior work has sought to characterize, detect, and mitigate memorization, the fundamental question of why and how it occurs remains unresolved. In this paper, we revisit the diffusion and denoising process and analyze latent space dynamics to address the question: "How do diffusion models memorize?" We show that memorization is driven by the overestimation of training samples during early denoising, which reduces diversity, collapses denoising trajectories, and accelerates convergence toward the memorized image. Specifically: (i) memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone, as training loss is larger under memorization due to classifier-free guidance amplifying predictions and inducing overestimation; (ii) memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, forcing latent trajectories to converge and steering denoising toward their paired samples; and (iii) a decomposition of intermediate latents reveals how initial randomness is quickly suppressed and replaced by memorized content, with deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule correlating almost perfectly with memorization severity. Together, these results identify early overestimation as the central underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models.

papers.title: Internal Representations of Vision Models Through the Lens of Frames on Data Manifolds
papers.research_question: How do model design choices (architecture, training algorithm) affect the hidden representation geometry and dynamics of deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces neural frames, a tool to study the small-scale geometry of neural representations, and uses it to make observations about how models process specific modes of variation.
papers.conclusion: Neural frames are a new tool that provides unique insights into how deep learning models interact with data manifolds, complementing existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Training with augmentation causes models to better preserve on-manifold augmentation frames, contradicting intuition that invariance would collapse such directions.
Adversarial training degrades preservation of augmentation frames but improves preservation of noise frames.
The stable rank of augmentation frames correlates with model accuracy.
Models preserve on-manifold tangent vectors and collapse off-manifold vectors.
Over the course of training, models initially compress the image manifold and then gradually expand it.
papers.limitation:
The frames used may only span a subspace of the tangent space, so changes orthogonal to the frame may be missed.
Augmentation frames may be challenging to define for specialized image manifolds where appropriate augmentations are not known.
future_direction: Tie the observations about manifold compression and expansion during training to the information bottleneck principle.
Investigate why transformers exhibit more fluctuation in stable rank compared to CNNs.
Develop methods for finding optimal frames for specific information extraction goals.
papers.abstract: While the last five years have seen considerable progress in understanding the internal representations of deep learning models, many questions remain. This is especially true when trying to understand the impact of model design choices, such as model architecture or training algorithm, on hidden representation geometry and dynamics. In this work we present a new approach to studying such representations inspired by the idea of a frame on the tangent bundle of a manifold. Our construction, which we call a neural frame, is formed by assembling a set of vectors representing specific types of perturbations of a data point, for example infinitesimal augmentations, noise perturbations, or perturbations produced by a generative model, and studying how these change as they pass through a network. Using neural frames, we make observations about the way that models process, layer-by-layer, specific modes of variation within a small neighborhood of a datapoint. Our results provide new perspectives on a number of phenomena, such as the manner in which training with augmentation produces model invariance or the proposed trade-off between adversarial training and model generalization.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2
papers.research_question: Do synthetic activations composed of SAE latents behave like real (model-generated) activations in terms of directional sensitivity and activation plateaus? What properties of SAE latents are important for this?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic activations composed of SAE latents can approximate real activations in directional sensitivity when controlling for sparsity and cosine similarity, but they fail to reproduce activation plateaus, indicating that real activations have additional structure beyond a simple bag of latents.
papers.conclusion: Model-generated activations cannot be explained by simple 'bags of SAE latents'; leveraging statistical and geometric properties of SAE latents helps create synthetic activations more similar to real ones in sensitivity, but these synthetic activations lack the characteristic activation plateaus, suggesting additional latent properties influence model computation.
papers.key_findings:
The 'bag of SAE latents' approach is insufficient to produce synthetic activations that resemble real activations.
Sparsity of the top SAE latent, relative latent activations, and cosine similarity between active latents and the top latent are important for synthetic activations to behave like real activations in sensitivity experiments.
Synthetic activations do not exhibit activation plateaus like real activations do.
SAE reconstructions of real activations behave similarly to real activations, indicating that SAE reconstruction error is not the main cause of the discrepancy.
The model is more sensitive to perturbations towards real activations than random directions, and synthetic-structured activations are more similar to real activations than synthetic-baseline activations in sensitivity experiments.
papers.limitation:
The heuristics for constructing synthetic activations leave room for improvement, as evidenced by the gap between them and model-generated activations, especially for activation plateaus.
The method uses cosine similarity between SAE latents to capture geometric relationships but does not account for latent co-occurrence and other relationships.
The synthetic activations do not match the cosine similarity distribution of SAE latents in model-generated activations closely.
The method leverages information from the base activation to construct synthetic activations (though verified that using a different activation does not change results).
The L2 distance curves exhibit significant variability, impacting the effectiveness of the maximum slope metric; more robust metrics could produce clearer results.
The study focuses solely on one layer of GPT2-small and perturbations confined to the final token position; generalizability to other layers, models, SAEs, and context lengths is not established.
future_direction: Developing better approaches to constructing synthetic activations that perform better in both experimental settings.
Checking for the existence of thresholds below which the model output does not respond to changes in latent activations.
Case studies looking at model sensitivity to perturbations in directions created using interpretable SAE latents and taking context into account.
papers.abstract: Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are commonly employed in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the residual stream into monosemantic SAE latents. Recent work demonstrates that perturbing a model's activations at an early layer results in a step-function-like change in the model's final layer activations. Furthermore, the model's sensitivity to this perturbation differs between model-generated (real) activations and random activations. In our study, we assess model sensitivity in order to compare real activations to synthetic activations composed of SAE latents. Our findings indicate that synthetic activations closely resemble real activations when we control for the sparsity and cosine similarity of the constituent SAE latents. This suggests that real activations cannot be explained by a simple "bag of SAE latents" lacking internal structure, and instead suggests that SAE latents possess significant geometric and statistical properties. Notably, we observe that our synthetic activations exhibit less pronounced activation plateaus compared to those typically surrounding real activations.

papers.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we find meaningful directions (concept vectors) in activation space that correspond to distinct features, starting from polysemantic neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors that represent distinct features, allowing for fine-grained concept separation controlled by a distance threshold.
papers.conclusion: Exploring directions in activation space (concept vectors) instead of individual neurons can lead to finding coherent fundamental units, bridging mechanistic interpretability and concept discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into concept vectors that are linear combinations of neurons.
The concept vectors encode coherent, human-understandable features, as validated by human experiments.
The method can separate fine-grained concepts (e.g., underwater scenes vs. scuba divers) by adjusting a distance threshold.
The latent space representations have higher similarity with the discovered concept vectors than with the neuron directions.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on the data used to generate clusters.
All experiments were performed on image data, which may limit generalizability to other data types.
future_direction: Generalizing the method to other data types such as language and tabular data.
Looking at other starting candidates for concepts besides neurons.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand how models store representations by breaking down neural networks into interpretable units. However, the occurrence of polysemantic neurons, or neurons that respond to multiple unrelated features, makes interpreting individual neurons challenging. This has led to the search for meaningful vectors, known as concept vectors, in activation space instead of individual neurons. The main contribution of this paper is a method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into concept vectors encapsulating distinct features. Our method can search for fine-grained concepts according to the user’s desired level of concept separation. The analysis shows that polysemantic neurons can be disentangled into directions consisting of linear combinations of neurons. Our evaluations show that the concept vectors found encode coherent, human-understandable features.

papers.title: Usable Information and Evolution of Optimal Representations During Training
papers.research_question: How do optimal (minimal and sufficient) representations emerge during training in deep networks, and what is the role of implicit regularization from SGD?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a notion of 'usable information' to study training dynamics, showing that SGD with high learning rate and small batch size leads to minimal sufficient representations through a dynamic process of acquiring and later discarding irrelevant information.
papers.conclusion: Usable information is a useful tool for studying training dynamics, revealing that SGD with specific hyperparameters leads to minimal representations through a dynamic process of acquiring and then discarding irrelevant information.
papers.key_findings:
SGD with random initialization leads to minimal sufficient representations in the checkerboard task and image classification.
Networks acquire semantically meaningful but irrelevant information early in training and later discard it to achieve minimality.
The learning dynamics (acquisition and forgetting) depend on hyperparameters like learning rate and batch size.
Pretraining on irrelevant information can prevent the formation of minimal representations and hurt generalization.
The phenomenon is observed in both simple perceptual tasks and standard image classification tasks with modern architectures.
papers.limitation: The usable information is estimated with a decoder network, which may not capture all information present in the representation.
future_direction: Investigate the tightness of the bound between usable information and mutual information.
Extend the approach to other tasks and architectures.
papers.abstract: We introduce a notion of usable information contained in the representation learned by a deep network, and use it to study how optimal representations for the task emerge during training. We show that the implicit regularization coming from training with Stochastic Gradient Descent with a high learning-rate and small batch size plays an important role in learning minimal sufficient representations for the task. In the process of arriving at a minimal sufficient representation, we find that the content of the representation changes dynamically during training. In particular, we find that semantically meaningful but ultimately irrelevant information is encoded in the early transient dynamics of training, before being later discarded. In addition, we evaluate how perturbing the initial part of training impacts the learning dynamics and the resulting representations. We show these effects on both perceptual decision-making tasks inspired by neuroscience literature, as well as on standard image classification tasks.

papers.title: Modelling Cellular Perturbations with the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action, combining compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SAMS-VAE, a generative model that combines sparsity, compositionality, and disentanglement for perturbation modeling, demonstrating improved predictive performance and interpretability on single-cell sequencing data.
papers.conclusion: SAMS-VAE is a useful model for perturbational screening data, with improved predictive performance and ability to recover factors correlated with biological mechanisms, and may aid in scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAMS-VAE with correlated inference achieves the best test IWELBO and average treatment effect correlation.
SAMS-VAE's latent mask is more predictive of annotated biological pathways than SVAE+.
SAMS-VAE and CPA-VAE perform well on out-of-distribution combinatorial tasks and in low-data settings.
SAMS-VAE improves prediction of nonlinear genetic interactions over a naive linear model.
Correlated inference strategies (correlated zbasal and correlated E) improve model performance.
papers.limitation: The prior on the mask may not enforce sparsity as desired when sample size increases, requiring adjustment of the prior strength to achieve desired sparsity.
future_direction: Studying how perturbations interact and compose in more complex fashion.
Incorporating different forms of prior knowledge into such systems.
papers.abstract: Generative models of observations under interventions have been a vibrant topic of interest across machine learning and the sciences in recent years. For example, in drug discovery, there is a need to model the effects of diverse interventions on cells in order to characterize unknown biological mechanisms of action. We propose the Sparse Additive Mechanism Shift Variational Autoencoder, SAMS-VAE, to combine compositionality, disentanglement, and interpretability for perturbation models. SAMS-VAE models the latent state of a perturbed sample as the sum of a local latent variable capturing sample-specific variation and sparse global variables of latent intervention effects. Crucially, SAMS-VAE sparsifies these global latent variables for individual perturbations to identify disentangled, perturbation-specific latent subspaces that are flexibly composable. We evaluate SAMS-VAE both quantitatively and qualitatively on a range of tasks using two popular single cell sequencing datasets. In order to measure perturbation-specific model-properties, we also introduce a framework for evaluation of perturbation models based on average treatment effects with links to posterior predictive checks. SAMS-VAE outperforms comparable models in terms of generalization across in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, including a combinatorial reasoning task under resource paucity, and yields interpretable latent structures which correlate strongly to known biological mechanisms. Our results suggest SAMS-VAE is an interesting addition to the modeling toolkit for machine learning-driven scientific discovery.

papers.title: Disentangled representations via score-based variational autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations without explicit supervision by combining diffusion models and variational autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAMI, a method that combines diffusion models and VAEs to learn disentangled representations without supervision, and can extract interpretable latent representations from pre-trained diffusion models.
papers.conclusion: Implicit structural information in diffusion models can be made explicit and interpretable through synergistic combination with a variational autoencoder.
papers.key_findings:
SAMI recovers ground truth generative factors in synthetic data.
It learns factorized, semantic latent dimensions from complex natural images.
It encodes video sequences into latent trajectories that are straighter than those of alternative encoders.
It can extract useful representations from pre-trained diffusion models with minimal additional training.
The probabilistic formulation allows identification of semantically meaningful axes without supervised labels.
papers.abstract: We present the Score-based Autoencoder for Multiscale Inference (SAMI), a method for unsupervised representation learning that combines the theoretical frameworks of diffusion models and VAEs. By unifying their respective evidence lower bounds, SAMI formulates a principled objective that learns representations through score-based guidance of the underlying diffusion process. The resulting representations automatically capture meaningful structure in the data: it recovers ground truth generative factors in our synthetic dataset, learns factorized, semantic latent dimensions from complex natural images, and encodes video sequences into latent trajectories that are straighter than those of alternative encoders, despite training exclusively on static images. Furthermore, SAMI can extract useful representations from pre-trained diffusion models with minimal additional training. Finally, the explicitly probabilistic formulation provides new ways to identify semantically meaningful axes in the absence of supervised labels, and its mathematical exactness allows us to make formal statements about the nature of the learned representation. Overall, these results indicate that implicit structural information in diffusion models can be made explicit and interpretable through synergistic combination with a variational autoencoder.

papers.title: Human-interpretable model explainability on high-dimensional data
papers.research_question: How to provide human-interpretable model explanations on high-dimensional data by using semantic latent features and adapting the Shapley framework.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for model explainability on high-dimensional data that encodes raw inputs into semantic latent features and applies Shapley explainability to these features, providing interpretable, theoretically-controlled explanations.
papers.conclusion: The framework offers a principled, flexible way to achieve human-interpretable explainability on complex models and is hoped to be widely applicable.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarially robust classifiers are less sensitive to high-frequency information compared to non-robust models.
Texture classification models depend on high-frequency periodic patterns in images.
Disentangled latent representations can correctly attribute model decisions to known factors of variation (e.g., scale and position in dSprites).
In CelebA, a model predicting attractiveness shows bias towards gender and age, as revealed by semantic explanations.
The framework provides interpretable explanations that are not possible with pixel-based methods.
papers.limitation: The quality of explanations depends on the semantic representation; if the representation is not well-disentangled, explanations may be corrupted.
papers.abstract: The importance of explainability in machine learning continues to grow, as both neural-network architectures and the data they model become increasingly complex. Unique challenges arise when a model's input features become high dimensional: on one hand, principled model-agnostic approaches to explainability become too computationally expensive; on the other, more efficient explainability algorithms lack natural interpretations for general users. In this work, we introduce a framework for human-interpretable explainability on high-dimensional data, consisting of two modules. First, we apply a semantically meaningful latent representation, both to reduce the raw dimensionality of the data, and to ensure its human interpretability. These latent features can be learnt, e.g. explicitly as disentangled representations or implicitly through image-to-image translation, or they can be based on any computable quantities the user chooses. Second, we adapt the Shapley paradigm for model-agnostic explainability to operate on these latent features. This leads to interpretable model explanations that are both theoretically controlled and computationally tractable. We benchmark our approach on synthetic data and demonstrate its effectiveness on several image-classification tasks.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a spectral filtering framework to disentangle scale-specific information in language model representations and a prism layer that trains models to specialize neurons for different scales, improving performance on long-range tasks.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques are a powerful set of tools for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can disentangle scale-specific information in BERT representations, with high-pass filters useful for word-level tasks and low-pass filters for document-level tasks.
The prism layer enables BERT to produce multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
Training with the prism layer increases the model's sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling.
The method is general and could be applied to other domains like images, audio, and video.
future_direction: Applying the spectral techniques to other domains such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning models.
Using the tools for interpretability research to better understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Applying the method to track topics over time in linguistic change research.
papers.abstract:
Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to
words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models
capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture
structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on
individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different
timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for
separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle
scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn
more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the
activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that
perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts
classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level),
while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for
training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to
model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better
predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale
representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our
methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language,
such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: Unsupervised Discovery of Interpretable Directions in h-space of Pre-trained Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How to discover interpretable directions in the h-space of pre-trained diffusion models in an unsupervised manner?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an unsupervised method to discover interpretable directions in the h-space of pre-trained diffusion models, and a VRAM-efficient training algorithm to enable training with many diffusion steps.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a general method to identify interpretable directions in the h-space of pre-trained diffusion models, and a VRAM-efficient training algorithm, with extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
The method discovers interpretable directions in h-space that correspond to semantic attributes (e.g., thickness, width, angle for MNIST; hair color, pose, etc. for face datasets).
The VRAM-efficient algorithm reduces memory usage while maintaining training efficiency, enabling training with many diffusion steps.
The discovered directions are global and scalable, allowing smooth transitions along the direction for all samples.
The method can edit real images by manipulating the h-space, validating the linearity property of h-space.
The adversarial training with a discriminator maintains the fidelity of shifted samples, as shown by FID scores.
papers.limitation:
Slow training and inference speed due to the iterative generative process of diffusion models.
The use of adversarial training to maintain fidelity might be replaced by simpler methods.
Potential negative impact of creating deepfakes.
future_direction: Exploring simpler methods to maintain the fidelity of shifted samples.
papers.abstract: We propose the first unsupervised and learning-based method to identify interpretable directions in h-space of pre-trained diffusion models. Our method is derived from an existing technique that operates on the GAN latent space. Specifically, we employ a shift control module that works on h-space of pre-trained diffusion models to manipulate a sample into a shifted version of itself, followed by a reconstructor to reproduce both the type and the strength of the manipulation. By jointly optimizing them, the model will spontaneously discover disentangled and interpretable directions. To prevent the discovery of meaningless and destructive directions, we employ a discriminator to maintain the fidelity of shifted sample. Due to the iterative generative process of diffusion models, our training requires a substantial amount of GPU VRAM to store numerous intermediate tensors for back-propagating gradient. To address this issue, we propose a general VRAM-efficient training algorithm based on gradient checkpointing technique to back-propagate any gradient through the whole generative process, with acceptable occupancy of VRAM and sacrifice of training efficiency. Compared with existing related works on diffusion models, our method inherently identifies global and scalable directions, without necessitating any other complicated procedures. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

papers.title: Enabling Local Editing in Diffusion Models by Joint and Individual Component Analysis
papers.research_question: How to achieve local image editing in diffusion models by factorizing the latent semantics of the denoising network into joint and individual components.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an unsupervised method for local image editing in diffusion models by decomposing the Jacobian of the denoising network into joint and individual components, enabling localized semantic manipulations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method enables localized semantic manipulation of real images using pre-trained diffusion models by factorizing latent subspaces, with discovered directions generalizing across images and outperforming previous methods.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies semantic directions in the latent space that are localized to specific image regions, enabling fine-grained editing.
Decomposing the Jacobian into joint and individual components disentangles global and local variations, allowing for edits that affect only the region of interest.
The discovered latent directions generalize from a single reference image to other images, making the method suitable for plug-and-play applications.
The method produces edits with higher fidelity and better localization compared to existing state-of-the-art alternatives, as measured by FID, ID, and ROIR metrics.
future_direction: Explore the latent semantics of video diffusion models.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Diffusion Models (DMs) have led to significant progress in visual synthesis and editing tasks, establishing them as a strong competitor to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). However, the latent space of DMs is not as well understood as that of GANs. Recent research has focused on unsupervised semantic discovery in the latent space of DMs by leveraging the bottleneck layer of the denoising network, which has been shown to exhibit properties of a semantic latent space. However, these approaches are limited to discovering global attributes. In this paper we address, the challenge of local image manipulation in DMs and introduce an unsupervised method to factorize the latent semantics learned by the denoising network of pre-trained DMs. Given an arbitrary image and defined regions of interest, we utilize the Jacobian of the denoising network to establish a relation between the regions of interest and their corresponding subspaces in the latent space. Furthermore, we disentangle the joint and individual components of these subspaces to identify latent directions that enable local image manipulation. Once discovered, these directions can be applied to different images to produce semantically consistent edits, making our method suitable for practical applications. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that our method can produce semantic edits that are more localized and have better fidelity compared to the state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Selectivity considered harmful: evaluating the causal impact of class selectivity in DNNs
papers.research_question: Is class selectivity in individual units necessary and/or sufficient for DNN function?
papers.core_contribution: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can even impair it; reducing selectivity can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can be detrimental. This encourages caution when focusing on single-unit properties and emphasizes distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
Reducing class selectivity can improve test accuracy, e.g., by over 2% for ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet.
Class selectivity can be reduced by a factor of 2.5 in ResNet20 on CIFAR10 with no impact on test accuracy, and nearly to zero with only a small drop.
Increasing class selectivity significantly decreases test accuracy across all models and datasets.
The regularizer suppresses selectivity generally, not just by rotating it off-axis, indicating viability of low-selectivity distributed representations.
Networks are at a performance cliff with regard to class selectivity; naturally learned levels are at the limit of what impairs performance.
papers.abstract: The properties of individual neurons are often analyzed in order to understand the biological and artificial neural networks in which they're embedded. Class selectivity-typically defined as how different a neuron's responses are across different classes of stimuli or data samples-is commonly used for this purpose. However, it remains an open question whether it is necessary and/or sufficient for deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn class selectivity in individual units. We investigated the causal impact of class selectivity on network function by directly regularizing for or against class selectivity. Using this regularizer to reduce class selectivity across units in convolutional neural networks increased test accuracy by over 2% for ResNet18 trained on Tiny ImageNet. For ResNet20 trained on CIFAR10 we could reduce class selectivity by a factor of 2.5 with no impact on test accuracy, and reduce it nearly to zero with only a small ($\sim$2%) drop in test accuracy. In contrast, regularizing to increase class selectivity significantly decreased test accuracy across all models and datasets. These results indicate that class selectivity in individual units is neither sufficient nor strictly necessary, and can even impair DNN performance. They also encourage caution when focusing on the properties of single units as representative of the mechanisms by which DNNs function.

papers.title: Canonical Latent Representations in Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify the underlying core categorical semantics in a conditional diffusion model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Canonical Latent Representations (CLAReps) in conditional diffusion models, which capture core class semantics with minimal irrelevant context, and a feature distillation paradigm (CaDistill) that uses CLAReps to improve student network robustness and generalization.
papers.conclusion: Conditional diffusion models can serve not only as image generators but also as compact, interpretable teachers that can drive robust representation learning through their canonical latent representations.
papers.key_findings:
CLARID identifies latent codes (CLAReps) whose internal CDM features preserve essential categorical information while discarding non-discriminative signals.
Decoded CLAReps produce Canonical Samples, which serve as interpretable and compact class prototypes.
The proposed feature distillation method, CaDistill, uses CLAReps to transfer core class knowledge, improving student adversarial robustness and generalization with only 10% of the training data size.
CLARID generalizes to different CDM architectures (e.g., DiT, Stable Diffusion) and diffusion samplers.
Feature clusters derived from CLAReps are more compact and separable than those from original samples, indicating better feature quality.
papers.limitation: CLARID can occasionally select suboptimal inversion time step (te) and number of extraneous directions (k), leading to artefacts in the generated Canonical Samples.
future_direction: Investigating how the semantic structure in text-conditioned models shapes the located CLAReps.
Exploring the use of pixel-space diffusion models on ImageNet for feature distillation.
Combining CaDistill with more sophisticated multi-layer feature distillation frameworks.
papers.abstract: Conditional diffusion models (CDMs) have shown impressive performance across a range of generative tasks. Their ability to model the full data distribution has opened new avenues for analysis-by-synthesis in downstream discriminative learning. However, this same modeling capacity causes CDMs to entangle the class-defining features with irrelevant context, posing challenges to extracting robust and interpretable representations. To this end, we identify Canonical LAtent Representations (CLAReps), latent codes whose internal CDM features preserve essential categorical information while discarding non-discriminative signals. When decoded, CLAReps produce representative samples for each class, offering an interpretable and compact summary of the core class semantics with minimal irrelevant details. Exploiting CLAReps, we develop a novel diffusion-based feature-distillation paradigm, CaDistill.
